## Department of Homeland Security
• 8 CFR Part 274a
• [CIS No. 2859-26; DHS Docket No. USCIS-2025-0271]
( printed page 65306)
## AGENCY:
U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, DHS.
## ACTION:
Final rule.
## SUMMARY:

On October 30, 2025, DHS published an interim final rule (IFR) that amended DHS regulations to end the practice of automatically extending the validity of employment authorization documents (Forms I-766 or EADs) for aliens who have timely filed an application to renew their EAD in certain employment authorization categories. This final rule responds to comments received on the IFR and reaffirms and finalizes the provisions of the IFR. Ending the automatic extension of EADs enhances benefit integrity and prioritizes the proper vetting and screening of aliens before granting a new period of employment authorization and/or a new EAD.
## DATES:
This final rule is effective on October 14, 2026.

## I. Executive Summary
## A. Basis and Purpose

DHS's mission is to safeguard the American people, our homeland, and our values with honor and integrity. In service of that mission, DHS protects the United States from threats by terrorists, criminals, smugglers, transnational criminal organizations, failed-state actors, and unpredictable lone offenders that constitute present and future threats to public safety and national security.

USCIS issues EADs to certain classes of aliens. These documents are valid for a specified period. Aliens who intend to continue their employment beyond the date specified on their EAD must generally file an application to renew their employment authorization and/or EAD.

The automatic extension of the validity of an EAD grants the alien the benefit of extending his or her expired employment authorization and/or EAD merely by filing a timely renewal EAD application and without first completing adjudicative review and related vetting, including resolution of any derogatory information identified during the vetting process. That is, the automatic extension allows for the granting of the benefit without USCIS first performing the following actions: an eligibility determination, completing vetting and screening checks, resolving potential hits of derogatory information in connection with the alien, and a determination that the employment authorization should be granted in the exercise of discretion, if applicable.

On October 30, 2025, DHS issued an IFR titled, “Removal of the Automatic Extension of Employment Authorization Documents,” with a request for comment. See 90 FR 48799 (Oct. 30, 2025). The IFR amended DHS regulations to end the practice of automatically extending the validity of EADs for aliens in certain employment authorization categories who timely filed an application to renew their EAD. After careful consideration of the public comments submitted in connection with the IFR, DHS is reaffirming and finalizing the IFR without changes. The rationale and reasoning provided in the preamble for the IFR remains unchanged with respect to the regulatory amendments, and DHS, therefore, adopts such reasoning also to support this final rule.

In reaffirming and finalizing the changes made in the IFR, the purpose of this rule remains the same as articulated in the IFR: to prioritize the proper vetting and screening of aliens and ensure continued eligibility before granting a new period of employment authorization and/or a new EAD by ending the practice of automatically extending the validity of employment authorization and/or EADs for certain employment authorization categories.

Ending the practice of providing automatic extensions of EADs is consistent with Section 16 of President Trump's directive in Executive Order (E.O.) 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion, which directs the Secretary of Homeland Security, in coordination with the Secretary of State and the Attorney General, to take all appropriate action to align any departmental activities with the policies set out by the President and to ensure, among others, “that employment authorization is provided in a manner consistent with section 274A of the Immigration and Nationality Act ( 8 U.S.C. 1324a ), and that employment authorization is not provided to any unauthorized alien in the United States.”  [ 1 ]

It is also consistent with Section 2 of E.O. 14161 , Protecting the United States From Foreign Terrorists and Other National Security and Public Safety Threats, which directs the Secretary of State, in coordination with the Secretary of Homeland Security, the Attorney General, and the Director of National Intelligence to “identify all resources that may be used to ensure that all aliens seeking admission to the United States, or who are already in the United States, are vetted and screened to the maximum degree possible.”  [ 2 ]
## B. Legal Authority

The legal basis of this rulemaking is found in section 103(a) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), 8 U.S.C. 1103(a) , which authorizes the Secretary to administer and enforce the immigration and nationality laws and establish such regulations as the Secretary deems necessary for carrying out such authority, and section 101(b)(1)(F) of the Homeland Security Act (HSA), 6 U.S.C. 111(b)(1)(F) , which establishes as a primary mission of DHS the duty to “ensure that the overall economic security of the United States is not diminished by efforts, activities, and programs aimed at securing the homeland.”
## C. Summary of the Major Provisions of the Regulatory Action
This final rule adopts the IFR as final, without any changes, after careful consideration of the comments received. Accordingly, DHS is adopting as final the following changes that the IFR has made:
• Revised the heading of 8 CFR 274a.13(d) to clearly indicate that the up-to-540-day automatic extension period only applies to renewal EAD applications filed before October 30, 2025.

• Added new 8 CFR 274a.13(e) . The new provision explains that, unless otherwise provided in 8 CFR 274a.13(d) , by law, or through a Federal Register notice for Temporary Protected Status (TPS)-related employment documentation, the validity period of an expired or expiring Employment Authorization Document and/or employment authorization will not be automatically extended by a renewal EAD application filed on or after October 30, 2025.

DHS explained in the IFR that the IFR did not impact the validity of EADs that were automatically extended prior to October 30, 2025. It also explained that the IFR did not impact automatic extensions of EADs and/or employment authorization provided by law or Federal Register notices, such as those for TPS applicants pursuant to section 244 of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1254a , and 8 CFR part 244 . [ 3 ]
This final rule similarly does not impact these provisions.
## D. Costs and Benefits

This final rule has been designated a “significant regulatory action” and economically significant as defined under section 3(f)(1) of E.O. 12866 , because its annual effects on the economy may exceed $100 million in any year of the analysis. Accordingly, this rule has been reviewed by the Office of Management and Budget (OMB).
( printed page 65308)

This final rule reaffirms and finalizes changes made by the IFR to DHS regulations to end the practice of automatically extending the validity of employment authorization documents (Forms I-766 or EADs) for aliens who have timely filed an application to renew their EAD in certain employment authorization categories. The purpose of this change is to prioritize the proper vetting and screening of aliens and ensure continued eligibility before granting a new period of employment authorization and/or a new EAD. This final rule does not affect the validity of EADs that were automatically extended prior to the IFR. In previous rules providing for the automatic extension of EADs based on the timely filing of a renewal EAD application, DHS attempted to stabilize aliens' earnings and avoid labor turnover costs of employers. However, as explained in the IFR, the Department has shifted focus to prioritizing public safety and national security, and ensuring that aliens continue to be eligible and merit a favorable exercise of discretion, as applicable, before being granted continued employment authorization. See 90 FR 48799 , 48816 (Oct. 30, 2025).

DHS has prepared two types of quantified estimates of the impacts generated by this final rule. For a single 18-month window (starting in May 2027) from about 20,000 to 33,000 EADs are estimated to lapse, based on several assumptions. This rule may result in some EAD holders incurring a loss of earnings (“reduced earnings”) because of USCIS process delays for renewal EAD applications, as under this rule there could be disruption to their earnings due to a lapsed EAD. Such earnings loss to aliens could comprise beneficial transfers to other U.S. workers if the substitution of the latter for the former is relatively frictionless. Additionally, to the extent this rule affects EAD holders' jobs going unfilled, there will be impacts to tax transfers from businesses and employees to the Federal Government. [ 4 ]

This rule will also generate labor turnover costs to businesses that employ the affected-lapsed EAD holders, as under this rule there would be a disruption to the EAD holders' employment authorization and/or document validity. In conducting these estimates DHS emphasizes that variation in factors involved in the impact, including impact processing times, filing volumes, the timing of renewal filings, and underlying benefit requests, will cause variation in the impacts.

Due to variation in future populations and process times, there is likely to be substantial variation in the impact estimates. For this reason, DHS develops wide ranges capturing a high and low bound for the estimates, in terms of the means (expected value). This rule is estimated to result in $138.1 million in lost productivity costs to employers that are not able to easily replace aliens with lapsed EADs, costs of $312.1 million to U.S. employers from potential labor turnover, transfers due to earnings changes worth $138.1 million from employment-authorized aliens to replacement workers and is expected to generate tax reduction impacts of $14.5 million over an 18-month period. Approximately 1,700 and 2,800 employers are estimated to be impacted.
Section V.B. provides an A-4 accounting statement supporting the analysis and the accompanying economic analysis details the data and methodology supporting the impact estimates.
## II. Background
## A. Legal Authority

The Secretary of Homeland Security's (Secretary) authority for the regulatory amendments made in this final rule are found in various sections of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1101 et seq., and the HSA, Public Law 107-296 , 116 Stat. 2135 (codified in part at 6 U.S.C. 101 et seq. ).

General authority for issuing this rule is found in section 103(a) of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1103(a) , which authorizes the Secretary to administer and enforce the immigration and nationality laws and establish such regulations as the Secretary deems necessary for carrying out such authority, as well as section 102 of the HSA, 6 U.S.C. 112 , which vests all of the functions of DHS in the Secretary and authorizes the Secretary to issue regulations. [ 5 ]
Further authority for this rule is found in:

• Section 208(d)(2) of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1158(d)(2) , which provides the Secretary with authority to grant employment authorization, in his or her discretion, to applicants for asylum if 180 days have passed since filing an application for asylum;

• Section 214 of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1184 , including section 214(a)(1) of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1184(a)(1) , which authorizes the Secretary to prescribe, by regulation, the time and conditions of the admission of nonimmigrants;

• Section 244(a)(1)(B) of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1254a(a)(1)(B) , which states that the Secretary shall authorize employment and provide evidence of employment authorization for aliens who have been granted Temporary Protected Status;
• Section 274A(b) of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1324a(b) , which provides for the employment verification system and outlines employment eligibility verification requirements;
• Section 274A(h)(3)(B) of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1324a(h)(3)(B) , which recognizes the Secretary's authority to extend employment authorization to aliens in the United States;  [ 6 ]
and

• Sections 100003(c) and 100012(a) of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Public Law 119-21 (July 4, 2025), which limit the validity period of any employment authorization for aliens granted TPS under section 244 of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1254a , to either a period of one year or for the duration of the designation of TPS, whichever is shorter.
## B. Automatic Extension of Employment Authorization and Documentation

Before November 2016, 8 CFR 274a.13(d) stated that USCIS would adjudicate an EAD application within 90 days of receipt. If USCIS did not adjudicate the EAD application within that timeframe, the alien was eligible to request an interim EAD with a validity period not to exceed 240 days. [ 7 ]
On November 18, 2016, as part of DHS's efforts to implement the American Competitiveness in the
( printed page 65309)

Twenty-first Century Act of 2000 (AC21), DHS published a final rule that eliminated Interim EADs and replaced them with a maximum 180-day automatic extension period for certain renewal applicants. [ 8 ]
## C. Increasing the Automatic Extension Period From a Maximum of 180 Days to a Maximum of 540 Days

Since the promulgation of the final rule authorizing up to 180-day automatic extension period for certain renewal EAD applicants, USCIS' ability to process both initial and renewal EAD applications within USCIS' targeted processing times was adversely impacted by a variety of temporary circumstances. [ 9 ]
In May 2022  [ 10 ]
and April 2024, [ 11 ]

DHS temporarily increased the automatic extension from up to 180 days to up to 540 days. The May 2022 and April 2024 temporary final rules were intended to reduce the number of renewal EAD applicants eligible for an automatic extension of their EAD validity under 8 CFR 274a.13(d) experiencing lapses in their employment authorization and/or EAD validity because of USCIS processing delays.
DHS also issued a final rule in December 2024  [ 12 ]

that indefinitely increased the up to 540-day automatic extension for certain applications pending on May 4, 2022, or properly filed on or after May 4, 2022. That rule was intended to reduce the effects of unknown future circumstances that could significantly impact EAD renewal processing times. [ 13 ]
## D. The 2025 Interim Final Rule Removed Automatic Extensions for Certain Employment Authorization Documents

The IFR amended DHS regulations to end the practice of automatically extending the validity of certain EADs. See 8 CFR 274a.13(e) . The IFR did not impact the automatic extensions already granted to renewal EAD applicants under 8 CFR 274a.13(d)(1) , if the renewal EAD application was filed before October 30, 2025. See 8 CFR 274a.13(d) . The IFR also did not impact automatic extensions otherwise provided by law or in an applicable Federal Register notice regarding procedures for renewing TPS-related employment documentation pursuant to section 244 of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1254a , and 8 CFR part 244 . 14
See 8 CFR 274a.13(e) .
The IFR made two changes to the regulations governing EAD, as discussed below.
## 1. Added New 8 CFR 274a.13(e)

The IFR added a new paragraph (e) that went into effect immediately with the publication of the IFR on October 30, 2025. With 8 CFR 274a.13(e) , DHS eliminated the practice of providing automatic extension periods for employment authorization and/or EAD validity for up to 540 days for renewal applications filed on or after October 30, 2025. Therefore, renewal EAD applicants no longer receive an up to 540-day automatic extension of their employment authorization and/or EAD validity if they file their application on or after October 30, 2025. See 8 CFR 274a.13(e) .

Except as otherwise provided by law, in 8 CFR 274a.13(d) , or in accordance with an applicable Federal Register notice regarding procedures for renewing TPS-related employment documentation, an alien's employment authorization and/or EAD validity will expire as explained in the following paragraphs:

For those aliens who are employment authorized incident to status under 8 CFR 274a.12(a) , unless otherwise provided by law, their EAD will expire on the day after the end validity date stated on the face of the EAD. See 8 CFR 274a.13(e)(1) . Because the alien's employment authorization is tied to the alien's status in the United States, the alien's employment authorization will not expire on the date indicated on the EAD. Instead, the alien's employment authorization will expire or terminate on the same date the alien's status in the United States expires or terminates.

For example, an alien in L-2 nonimmigrant status as the spouse of an L-1 nonimmigrant is employment authorized incident to status. See INA sec. 214(c)(2)(E), 8 U.S.C. 1184(c)(2)(E) . If the L-2 nonimmigrant chooses to apply for an EAD to evidence his or her employment authorization, the EAD will expire as of the date indicated on the face of the EAD. In some cases that may be the same date as the expiration of the L-2's nonimmigrant status. But in other cases, the L-2 status expiration date may be after the EAD expiration date, particularly if the L-2 nonimmigrant travelled outside of the United States after obtaining an EAD and, upon return to the United States, was provided a new status expiration date that will expire after the EAD expires. [ 15 ]

In that scenario, the L-2 nonimmigrant would remain employment authorized while in L-2 nonimmigrant status, even after the EAD expires, but the expired EAD would no longer be a valid document to evidence the L-2 nonimmigrant's employment authorization. [ 16 ]

Once the alien is no longer in L-2 status (for example, the L-2 nonimmigrant status expires), the alien would no longer be employment authorized as an L-2 nonimmigrant because such employment authorization is dependent on being in L-2 nonimmigrant status.

For aliens who are not employment authorized incident to their immigration status and who instead must obtain employment authorization from USCIS, pursuant to 8 CFR 274a.12(c) before accepting employment in the United States, such as adjustment of status applicants or aliens with a pending asylum application, USCIS determines the length of the period of employment authorization in the exercise of its discretion and thereafter issues an EAD reflecting the validity period. [ 17 ]
Therefore, the EAD will expire and the employment authorization will terminate the day after the end validity
( printed page 65310)

date stated on the face of the EAD based upon the situations outlined in 8 CFR 274a.14 , or for aliens with employment authorization under 8 CFR 274a.12(c)(19) based on a pending TPS application, pursuant to section 244 of the Act and 8 CFR part 244   18

For example, an alien with a pending adjustment of status application (Form I-485) has an EAD that expires on May 30, 2026. The alien's adjustment of status application has not been adjudicated and continues to be pending. The alien is eligible to apply for a renewal EAD based on the pending adjustment of status application. The alien applies for a renewal of the EAD on February 4, 2026, which is after the October 30, 2025, effective date of the IFR. The alien will maintain continuous employment authorization if his or her renewal application is granted before his or her current employment authorization expires on May 30, 2026. If the renewal EAD application remains unadjudicated on May 31, 2026, the alien cannot continue to work for his or her employer on or after May 31, 2026, unless the alien is employment authorized on a separate basis. See 8 CFR 274a.13(e) . If the renewal EAD application is subsequently approved, the alien would again be employment authorized and may resume employment during the validity period stated on the new EAD. The longer an alien waits to file a renewal EAD application, the more likely it is that he or she may experience a temporary lapse in his or her employment authorization and/or EAD validity.
## 2. Modified the Heading of 8 CFR 274a.13(d)

On December 13, 2024, DHS published a final rule amending 8 CFR 274a.13(d) to permanently increase the automatic extension period for certain employment authorization and/or EAD validity. The rule became effective on January 13, 2025. [ 19 ]

DHS is retaining the provision granting an automatic extension for those aliens who had timely filed a renewal EAD request before October 30, 2025, and who otherwise meet the requirements of 8 CFR 274a.13(d) . The IFR amended 8 CFR 274a.13(d) by revising the paragraph's heading to reflect that the paragraph applies to renewal requests properly filed before October 30, 2025, to avoid confusion between the automatic extension period granted under 8 CFR 274a.13(d) for those renewal EAD requests filed prior to October 30, 2025, and those filed on the day of or after the publication of the IFR. With this final rule, DHS is adopting and finalizing the changes made by the IFR and not making any additional changes to the regulations.

This change to the heading of 8 CFR 274a.13(d) ensures that the IFR and this rule do not retroactively affect those aliens who have already timely and properly filed a renewal EAD application before October 30, 2025. For these aliens, an EAD that appears on its face to be expired (“facially expired”) is considered unexpired under this rule for up to 540 days from the expiration date on the front of the EAD when combined with a Notice of Action (Form I-797C) indicating timely filing (that is, the receipt notice for the Form I-765 issued by USCIS has a receipt date that is before the expiration date on the EAD and before October 30, 2025) of the renewal application based on the same employment eligibility category as stated on the facially expired EAD (or in the case of an EAD and I-797C notice) that contains either an A12 or C19 category code, the category codes need not match). In those cases, the alien's facially expired EAD is considered unexpired for up to 540 days from the expiration date on the face of the EAD. [ 20 ]
USCIS updated the web page on the USCIS website with the appropriate information. [ 21 ]
USCIS also updated I-9 Central on the USCIS website and the Handbook for Employers, M-274, to provide employers and employees with additional guidance. [ 22 ]
## E. Severability

In issuing this final rule, like the IFR, DHS continues to intend that the rule's various provisions be considered severable from one another to the greatest extent possible. For instance, if a court of competent jurisdiction were to hold that ending the practice of automatically extending the validity of employment authorization and/or EADs for aliens who have timely filed an application to renew their employment authorization and/or EAD in certain employment categories may only be applied to a particular category of renewal EAD applicants or in a particular circumstance, DHS would intend for the court to leave the remainder of the rule in place with respect to all other covered persons and circumstances. DHS's overarching goal is to militate against threats to national security and public safety and to ensure that employment authorization and/or EADs are provided only after USCIS conducts adequate vetting and determines that the alien continues to be eligible and merits a favorable exercise of discretion, if applicable.
## III. Changes in the Final Rule
This final rule adopts as final, without change, the amendments to 8 CFR 274a.13(d) and (e) in the IFR, published on October 30, 2025, at 90 FR 48799 .
## IV. Response to Public Comments on the Interim Final Rule
## A. Summary of Comments

When issuing the IFR, DHS invited the public to participate in the rulemaking by submitting post-promulgation comments on every aspect of the rule. DHS provided a 33-day comment period following the publication of the IFR. DHS received 653 public comment submissions in the Federal eRulemaking Portal site under Docket ID Number USCIS-2025-0271  [ 23 ]
in response to the rulemaking.

Comments were submitted by a range of entities and individuals, including attorneys and legal service providers, applicants, individual commenters, professional organizations, unions, advocacy groups, religious organizations, research and community organizations, and State and local government agencies or elected officials. Some commenters expressed support for the rule or offered suggestions for improvement. Some expressed general opposition to the rule, and some offered alternatives. For some of the public
( printed page 65311)
comments, DHS could not ascertain whether the commenter supported or opposed the IFR. Finally, some commenters addressed topics outside the scope of this rulemaking.
DHS carefully reviewed all the public comments received in response to the IFR and addresses relevant comments in this final rule, grouped by subject area.
## B. Comments in Support of the Rule

Comment: Several commenters supported the rule based on national security concerns, citing the need for proper vetting of nonimmigrant workers. Specifically, they stated that the rule would allow for thorough vetting of nonimmigrants before DHS extends their authorization to work in the United States. Commenters called the rule a “critical” measure to support the safety and security of the public. One commenter emphasized that working in the United States is a privilege, not a right, while another said that safety and national security should be government's highest priority.

Several commenters supported the rule based on concerns about fraud and abuse in the visa system, stating, for example, that it would help deter potential fraud and abuse by preventing aliens from remaining in the workforce for extended periods without final adjudication of their eligibility.

Multiple commenters supported the rule based on concerns about protecting job opportunities for American citizens. A commenter stated that automatic extensions keep nonimmigrant workers employed without timely reevaluation, allowing them to compete with American workers for positions while requiring renewed authorization before continuing employment ensures that only eligible aliens remain in the workforce.

Response: DHS agrees that this rule safeguards the process to fully evaluate the applicants in order to determine continued eligibility, identify national security and public safety concerns, and enhance fraud prevention through robust vetting and screening processes. This administration prioritizes the safety of the American people. Ensuring that employment authorization and/or EADs are provided only after USCIS conducts adequate vetting and determines that the alien continues to be eligible and merits a favorable exercise of discretion, if applicable, better protects national security, public safety, and the integrity of the immigration system. This rule is part of a larger DHS effort to reduce frivolous, fraudulent, and otherwise non-meritorious EAD filings and focus adjudicatory and other resources on ensuring national security and program integrity.
## C. Comments in Opposition to the Rule and Mixed Comments
## 1. DHS Legal Authority
## i. DHS Statutory Authority and Congressional Intent

Comment: Multiple commenters requested that the rule be withdrawn stating that the rule contradicts DHS's statutory mandate, including the mandate to ensure that “the overall economic security of the United States is not diminished by efforts . . . aimed at securing the homeland” under 6 U.S.C. 111(b)(1)(F) . Many of these commenters stated that, consistent with this statutory mandate, DHS recently concluded that a 540-day automatic EAD extension was necessary to protect employers and workers from lapses in work authorization due to USCIS delays, and DHS previously found that even the 180-day extension established under the 2016 Final Rule was not enough time to avoid harmful gaps in work authorization.

Response: DHS disagrees that this rule is inconsistent with DHS's statutory mandate, including the mandate under 6 U.S.C. 111(b)(1)(F) . According to 6 U.S.C. 111(b) , DHS's primary mission includes preventing terrorist attacks within the United States, reducing the vulnerability of the United States to terrorism, minimizing the damage, and assisting in the recovery, from terrorist attacks that occur within the United States, and ensuring that the overall economic security of the United States is not diminished by efforts, activities, and programs aimed at securing the homeland. See 6 U.S.C. 111(b)(1)(A) , (B), (C), and (F). While the provision does not specifically define “economic security,” another provision within 6 U.S.C. Chapter 1 (Homeland Security Organization), defines “economic security” as the “condition of having secure and resilient domestic production capacity, combined with reliable access to the global resources necessary to maintain an acceptable standard of living and to protect core national values.” See 6 U.S.C. 474(c)(2) . [ 24 ]

In addition, DHS is charged with the implementation of section 274A of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1324a , preventing unlawful employment of aliens. This rule, which is part of an effort to secure the homeland, supports DHS's mission as provided by Congress in 6 U.S.C. 111(b) and section 274A of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1324a , ensures lawful employment, and supports the overall national and economic security of the United States.

Ending the practice of providing automatic extension of employment authorization and/or EADs enhances the benefit integrity in adjudications of employment authorization requests and better protects public safety and national security by ensuring that aliens are properly vetted and determined to be eligible (and merit a favorable exercise of discretion, if applicable), for employment authorization before such authorization is provided to the alien. The automatic extension of an EAD grants the benefit of extending an alien's expired employment authorization and/or EAD merely by filing a timely renewal EAD application and without first completing adjudicative review and related vetting, including resolution of any derogatory information identified during the vetting process. That is, the benefit is granted without USCIS first performing the following actions: an eligibility determination, completing vetting and screening checks, resolving potential hits of derogatory information in connection with the alien, and a determination that the employment authorization should be renewed in the exercise of discretion, if applicable. Without the IFR and this final rule, aliens could still obtain an automatic extension despite derogatory information that could flag them as national security or public safety risks. Automatic extensions, therefore, pose a security risk.

DHS is charged with combating unauthorized employment in accordance with section 274A of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1324a , which Congress implemented, among other reasons, because of the detrimental negative effect that unauthorized employment and illegal immigration has on the United States and the national economy. [ 25 ]
Sections 103 and 274A of
( printed page 65312)

the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1103(a) and 8 U.S.C. 1324a , among other provisions, provide DHS and USCIS with considerable flexibility to administer and enforce the INA, including granting employment authorization and the issuance of an EAD. There is no generally applicable statutory mandate that requires DHS to provide an automatic extension. As explained in the IFR, the automatic extension carries the risk that employers unwittingly continue to employ a worker whose employment authorization is in fact no longer valid. See 90 FR at 48810. This includes that aliens may no longer be entitled to employment authorization because they no longer have an underlying status which entitles them to work. Additionally, vetting every alien before granting an immigration benefit, including employment authorization, has been one of the key considerations of Congress. [ 26 ]

The rule does not eliminate employment authorizations or prevent eligible aliens from obtaining EADs for employment purposes or proof of identity; or from seeking and maintaining authorized employment. The rule does not reduce economic security. To the contrary, the rule supports the condition of having secure and resilient domestic production capacity, and protects core national values, as directed by Congress, with U.S. workers who are legally authorized to work. Therefore, the IFR is consistent with DHS's statutory mandate, including the mandate at 6 U.S.C. 111(b)(1)(F) , because it appropriately balances the need for security and vetting while maintaining overall EAD eligibility practices.

DHS is cognizant that prior rulemakings stated that DHS believed, at the time, that taking immediate action and providing automatic extensions of employment authorization supported USCIS' (as a component of DHS) statutory mission to administer employment authorization effectively, and as a measure to ensure that the overall economic security was not diminished by potentially harmful gaps in employment authorizations. See, e.g., 89 FR 101208 , 101209 (Dec. 13, 2024); 89 FR 24628 , 24629 and 24651 (Apr. 8, 2024). As explained in this response, and throughout this rule, DHS believes that the factual situation underlying prior rules, in particular the Dec. 13, 2024 rule, have significantly changed, including that DHS has taken significant steps to reduce the flood of filings of EADs that overwhelmed USCIS' adjudicative resources. [ 27 ]
Furthermore, the 2024 final rule made the automatic extension period permanent based on the presumption that harmful gaps would occur given the operational realities at the time. [ 28 ]

Even if the 2024 final rule had taken into account the security posture of the United States, it was unclear how the rule furthered the economic security given that the rule was based on potential harm to individual applicants and their employers, rather than the broader national economy. It is thus unclear how removing the automatic extension period, which improves the security posture of the United States and is consistent with immigration laws, would undermine the overall economic security of the United States.
Comment: A commenter asserted that removing the automatic extension of employment authorization without ensuring timely adjudication would strip lawfully authorized noncitizens  [ 29 ]

of their ability to work due to USCIS processing delays, which, according to the commenter, contradicts the intent of the INA and the “right” to work in the United States. Another commenter stated that the IFR incorrectly states that the rule is consistent with section 274A of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1324a . Another commenter stated that it seems illegal to deny someone a renewal when they have followed the law and have filed the renewal application in a timely manner.

Response: DHS disagrees with these commenters' assertions. This final rule and the IFR are consistent with section 274A of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1324a , which, among other things, recognizes the Secretary's authority to grant employment authorization in his or her discretion. DHS disagrees with the commenter's assertion that aliens have a broadly applicable “right” to work in the United States. Rather, the INA makes clear that aliens, to lawfully work in the United States, must be so authorized by law or a grant of employment authorization by the Secretary. See INA 274A(h)(3), 8 U.S.C. 1324a(h)(3) . Contrary to the commenters' assertions, this rule does not impact whether DHS will renew an alien's employment authorization; it only removes an intermediate automatic extension of the EAD period. If DHS determines that the alien is eligible for continued employment authorization and merits a favorable exercise of discretion, as applicable, DHS may grant the renewal of employment authorization. This final rule merely ends the practice of automatically granting the benefit of continued employment authorization without USCIS first performing the following actions: eligibility determination, completing vetting and screening checks, resolving potential hits of derogatory information in connection with the alien, and a determination that the employment authorization should be granted in the exercise of discretion, if applicable.
Comment: A commenter stated that, when providing the ability for asylum
( printed page 65313)

seekers to obtain work authorization, Congress could not have intended the arbitrary and capricious impact, on both the alien authorized to work and the employer who has relied on that alien, of being without authorization for an indeterminate amount of time until USCIS adjudicates either the asylum application or a new EAD. A commenter stated, without pointing to specific provisions, that the IFR should be discontinued because its policy changes do not reflect the law or the intent of the law or even the will of the people who voted for candidates who would make immigration changes.

Response: DHS disagrees with the commenters' assertion. Section 208(d)(2) of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1158(d)(2) , expressly states that “[a]n applicant for asylum is not entitled to employment authorization,” though it also provides the Secretary with authority to grant employment authorization, in his or her discretion, to applicants for asylum if 180 days have passed since filing an application for asylum. The IFR, and this final rule, clearly outline the legal authority for this change, and are consistent with the Secretary's discretionary authority regarding the grant of employment authorization for asylum applicants and the duration of such authorization.
## ii. Constitutional Concerns

Comment: Multiple commenters expressed that the IFR raises First Amendment concerns, because the IFR suggests that USCIS must evaluate whether renewal applicants “bear hostile attitudes” toward U.S. citizens, culture, government, institutions, or founding principles. The commenters reasoned that employment authorization may not be conditioned on ideological conformity and that agency action on unconstitutional factors may not be sustained as it is constitutionally questionable and impermissible. Another commenter stated that an ideological screening regime for work authorization renewals would further entrench USCIS in DHS's “troubling pattern” of suppressing First Amendment rights in the name of national security and opens the door for USCIS to profile individuals.

Response: DHS disagrees with the commenters. Citizens and aliens may object to various statutes, regulations, and policies and express those objections publicly. This rule neither penalizes individuals for protected political beliefs or associations nor subjects them to activities such as ideological screenings or profiling. This rule does not abridge the freedom of speech, of the press, or of association or peaceful assembly. Rather, it ends the practice of automatically granting the benefit of continued employment authorization without USCIS concurrently performing the following actions: eligibility determination, completing vetting and screening checks, resolving potential hits of derogatory information in connection with the alien, or a determination that the employment authorization should be renewed in the exercise of discretion, if applicable.

DHS notes that freedom of speech for aliens is not absolute. See, e.g., INA sec. 212(a)(3)(B)(i)(VII), 8 U.S.C. 1182(a)(3)(B)(i)(VII) (stating that any alien who endorses or espouses terrorist activity, or persuades others to endorse or espouse terrorist activity or support a terrorist organization, is inadmissible), and INA sec. 212(a)(6)(C)(ii), 8 U.S.C. 1182(a)(6)(C)(ii) (stating that any alien who falsely represents, or has falsely represented, himself or herself to be a citizen of the United States for any purpose or benefit under Federal or State law is inadmissible). DHS has a compelling interest in vetting and screening aliens before granting a benefit request, particularly when such request is granted in USCIS' discretion, as applicable.

DHS also notes that a challenge to the First Amendment cannot lie unless an individual establishes that he or she faces a “credible threat of prosecution” specifically for his or her speech, “under a statute [or rule] that appears to render the [individual]'s arguably protected speech illegal.” See, e.g., Am. Library Ass'n v. Barr, 956 F.2d 1178, 1194 (D.C. Cir. 1992). As indicated above, that is not the case in this scenario as neither section 274A of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1324a , nor the associated regulations, renders any form of speech illegal or attempts to directly or indirectly regulate or penalize speech. Rather, the IFR and this final rule subject all EAD renewal applicants to the same vetting and screening procedures used for initial applications or those applicants who were not previously eligible for an automatic extension of their renewal employment authorization and/or EAD.

Comment: Several commenters raised concerns related to due process. Referencing the Fifth Amendment, a commenter stated that the IFR undermines the right to due process and the right to seek asylum by eliminating automatic extensions, which will cause large numbers of asylum seekers and other immigrants to lose employment authorization through no fault of their own. Another commenter said the rule replaces due process with guilt by association and abandons any pretense of a fair and rational immigration system. Other commenters expressed concerns about due process related to the immediate effective date of the IFR, stating that implementation of the IFR appears to be designed to reflect and further the current administration's policies and efforts toward “creating and enhancing chaos and dysfunction.”

Response: DHS disagrees with the commenters' assertions that the IFR, and this final rule by virtue of reaffirming and finalizing the IFR, undermine due process or the ability of aliens to request asylum, or that it will cause large numbers of asylum seekers or other aliens to lose employment authorization.

In general, the Fifth Amendment of the U.S. Constitution protects due process rights to a government benefit if the alien has an entitlement to it, but a benefit is not a protected entitlement if government officials may grant or deny it in their discretion. See Town of Castle Rock, Colorado v. Gonzales, 545 U.S. 748, 756 (2005). There is no generally applicable statutory mandate to grant automatic extensions of employment authorizations. DHS and USCIS have been provided with considerable flexibility and discretion under section 103 and 274A of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1103(a) and 8 U.S.C. 1324a , among other provisions, to administer and enforce the INA, including granting employment authorization. Therefore, there is generally no cognizable due process interest in matters related to automatic extensions of employment authorizations and/or EADs. Additionally, contrary to the commenter's assertion, the rule does not suggest guilt by association or that the immigration system is unfair or irrational. A fair and rational immigration system ensures that aliens are sufficiently vetted, and any background hits are resolved before a determination is made that the alien is eligible for an extension of his or her employment authorization and/or an EAD and merits a favorable exercise of discretion, as applicable. The examples provided in the IFR do not suggest guilt by association. Rather, those examples highlight the importance and urgency of ensuring that aliens are not granted employment authorization until appropriate adjudicative review has been completed, and the risks to the national security and public safety if such benefits are granted automatically.
DHS also disagrees with the assertion that immediate implementation of the IFR was designed or intended to create chaos or dysfunction. DHS explained in the IFR why it was implementing the
( printed page 65314)

rule with immediate effect. DHS concluded that the good cause exceptions in 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B) and (d)(3) apply to the IFR and that delaying the implementation of the IFR until the conclusion of notice and comment procedures and the delayed effective date would be impracticable and contrary to public interest. See 90 FR 48814 (Oct. 30, 2025). DHS also explained that the IFR was issued with an immediate effective date because the rule clearly implicates the foreign affairs policy of the United States, and that notice and comment procedure as well as a 30-day delayed effective date would result in undesirable international consequences. See 90 FR 48816 (Oct. 30, 2025).
## iii. International Law and Refugee Protections
Comment: Several commenters stated that the IFR violates refugee protections, including the 1967 Protocol Relating to the Status of Refugees and the Refugee Act of 1980. [ 30 ]

One of these commenters said the Refugee Act of 1980 specifically enshrines the right of refugees to work, obtain documentation, and access education, and UNHCR Guidance makes clear that asylum seekers awaiting adjudication of their cases are to be afforded the right to work. The commenter said asylum seekers must obtain EADs to work while their cases are pending, and gaps in EADs restrict the enjoyment of these rights either by directly impacting the right to safe work, or because many services require documentation for which an EAD may be the only form of proof available.

Another commenter stated that eliminating the automatic extension was contrary to Article 34 of the 1951 Refugee Convention, because the resulting loss of employment and the bar of legal employment impede assimilation and naturalization of refugees. The commenter also said the IFR was contrary to Article 33's nonrefoulement, and the Refugee Convention's and Protocol's mandate to facilitate access to fair and efficient refugee status determination procedures that function as a safeguard against refoulement. The commenter reasoned that by undermining asylum seekers' ability to meet their basic needs through legal employment while their claims are pending, the rule obstructs access to a fair asylum procedure and risks forcing aliens to abandon their claims, potentially resulting in their return to the country of persecution.
A commenter stated that cutting off work authorization from people fleeing persecution contradicts our legal obligations and longstanding values.

Response: DHS disagrees that ending the practice of granting automatic extensions for EAD renewals is inconsistent with the United States' international obligations related to refugee protections, including the Refugee Convention and its Protocol and the Refugee Act of 1980. Although the United States is party to the 1967 Protocol, which incorporates, among others, Articles 17, 33, and 34 of the 1951 Refugee Convention, the treaty is not self-executing and is not directly enforceable in U.S. law. It is the domestic implementing law that governs. The Supreme Court and other case law makes clear that the Protocol serves only as a useful guide in determining congressional intent in enacting the Refugee Act of 1980, because the Act sought to bring U.S. law into conformity with the Protocol. See, e.g., INS v. Stevic, 467 U.S. 407, 428 n.22 (1984); Khan v. Holder, 584 F.3d 773, 783 (9th Cir. 2009). The United States Congress implemented U.S. obligations with respect to certain provisions of the Refugee Convention in the Refugee Act of 1980, including in sections 208, 235, and 241 of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1158 , 1225 and 1231 , and DHS regulations, including 8 CFR part 208 and 1208 . Section 208(d)(2) of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1158(d)(2) , provides the Secretary with authority to grant employment authorization, in his or her discretion, to applicants for asylum if 180 days have passed since filing an application for asylum.

The IFR is limited in scope, merely ending the practice of automatically extending the validity of employment authorization and/or EADs for aliens who have timely filed an application to renew their EAD in certain employment categories. There is no mandate under international or United States law that DHS provide an automatic extension of employment authorization and/or EAD validity for aliens filing renewal EAD applications, and certainly not without adequately being vetted for continued eligibility. Aliens with a pending asylum application are permitted to still apply for employment authorization as nothing in this rule restricts the ability to apply for an EAD. [ 31 ]

Rather, the IFR, and this final rule, are consistent with the Secretary's discretionary authority regarding the grant of employment authorization for asylum applicants and the duration of such authorization, and with international obligations, including the favorable treatment of those seeking refuge from persecution in their countries. DHS finally notes that asylees (but not those with pending asylum applications), refugees, and certain other aliens are “qualified aliens” for purpose of receiving public benefits to cover basic needs under Title IV of the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act of 1996. [ 32 ]
Therefore, even if there are gaps in employment on account of adjudication delays, these aliens may be able to obtain public benefits.

Comment: A commenter referenced Article 17 of the Refugee Convention, which provides that refugees lawfully in the territory of the host state (which would include not only asylees and resettled refugees, but all aliens pursuing asylum claims who apply for renewal EADs), shall be the accorded the “most favorable treatment accorded to nationals of a foreign country in the same circumstances.” The commenter stated that, because the rule does not end all automatic extensions of the validity period of EADs for those applying for renewal (for example, TPS-based EAD validity extensions through FRN), it provides refugees applying to renew their EADs less favorable treatment than other foreign nationals. The commenter concluded that the rule is therefore issued in violation of Article 17 of the Refugee Convention and should be withdrawn.
( printed page 65315)

Response: DHS disagrees with the commenters. The United States implemented the “Wage-earning and Employment” provision of Article 17 of the 1951 Refugee Convention (as incorporated through the 1967 Protocol) through sections 207 and 208 of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1157 , 1158 , and implementing regulations at 8 CFR 207 , 208 and 274a . Refugees (and asylees)  [ 33 ]

have the right to employment authorization upon arrival, with minimal restrictions and are provided a pathway to lawful permanent residency because their status in the United States is permanent. This approach aligns with Article 17's requirements and complies with the U.S. obligation including that these individuals are not subject to more restrictive conditions than other foreign nationals in similar circumstances. Even if Article 17 were imposing a binding obligation, nothing in Article 17 requires DHS to provide employment authorization to noncitizens seeking refugee status or asylum before DHS or an immigration judge has made a final determination that they meet requirements for asylum or refugee status and grant the alien's application.

TPS applicants do not have the same protections and legal definition as refugees and asylees. Aliens granted TPS and TPS applicants are only temporarily in the United States on account of the Secretary's designation under section 244 of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1254a , and 8 CFR part 244 . As part of the TPS statute, Congress provided employment authorization for purposes of the entire designation period. See INA sec. 244(a)(1)(B) and (2), 8 U.S.C. 1254a(a)(1)(B) and (2) . To comply with the law enacted by Congress, DHS is typically extending employment authorization via a Federal Register notice. However, TPS applicants still must apply for the renewal employment authorization document as part of the redesignation to obtain evidence of employment. Additionally, TPS may be terminated, and TPS never leads to permanent residency. See INA sec. 244(b)(3)(B), (h), 8 U.S.C. 1254a(b)(3)(B) , (h). Thus, upon termination of TPS, TPS beneficiaries and applicants may lose employment authorization in the United States. See 8 CFR 244.12 and 13 . Refugees (and asylees) once granted, do not typically lose their refugee status and thus, their right to employment and path to lawful permanent residency and eventually citizenship. Therefore, the implementation scheme and the termination of automatic extension is not contrary to the United States international obligations.
## 2. DHS Justification and Need for the Rule
## i. Security Rationale for the Rule
## a. General Security Rationale Comments
Comment: Multiple commenters said the IFR rests on a single asserted justification: the desire to complete vetting and security checks before approving an individual's  [ 34 ]

work permit renewal, and DHS offers no other policy rationale for eliminating automatic extensions. Commenters stated the IFR is a reversal in policy without new evidence or a reasoned explanation and violates the APA. The commenters stated that DHS's sole rationale suffers from numerous problems and reveals a significant mismatch between the concern asserted and the real-world purpose and impact of automatic extensions.
